summary:
The District of Columbia stands under the United States national framework, and travel documents are the sharpest exposure for a trans visitor. Executive Order 14168, signed 20 January 2025, redefined sex for federal purposes as a male-female binary, barred transgender people from government-funded single-sex facilities congruent with their gender identity, prohibited self-selection of gender on passports and visas, and directed the attorney general to "correct the misapplication" of Bostock v. Clayton County (2020). The State Department stopped processing the X marker and any marker not matching sex assigned at birth; new passport applications are processed only as M or F according to supporting documents, and passports already issued with an X marker remain valid until they expire. The Supreme Court in November 2025 allowed the passport sex-marker restrictions to take effect, superseding a State Department policy in place since 1992.

Trans and nonbinary travellers report passports confiscated or blocked at application, with some left stranded abroad. The ACLU has sued the State Department on behalf of seven plaintiffs, and Lambda Legal maintains guidance on what documentation to consider and how name and gender changes interact with federal records.

Screening at US checkpoints carries an outing risk: TSA procedures can involve secondary screening, devices and pat-downs that are invasive of privacy. Multiple foreign governments have responded. In April 2025 CNN reported that several countries issued advisories about trans people travelling to the United States over identity-document and data rules; Axios reported in March 2025 that at least eight European countries, including Finland and Denmark, adjusted travel guidelines for trans and nonbinary citizens entering the US.

Facilities access is restricted in a growing number of states. A Movement Advancement Project tally counts state bathroom bans applying to trans people in K-12 schools and some government buildings in nine states and one territory, with outright state bans on facility use per gender identity in additional states; 29 states, four territories and the District of Columbia have no such ban, and some states make trans bathroom use a criminal offence in certain circumstances. In April 2025 a transgender student was arrested and handcuffed in a women's restroom at the Florida state capitol in what civil-rights attorneys described as the first known arrest under that state's bathroom-restriction law.

State document rules are tightening. In February 2026 Kansas enacted a law preventing transgender people from changing markers on birth certificates and driver's licences and invalidating existing documents that do not match sex assigned at birth, and barring trans people from sex-segregated facilities; rights groups call it a template for other states, with further targeting bills pending in state legislatures. A July 2026 national risk assessment flagged Idaho as the latest "Do Not Travel" state for trans people, bringing the total to four states so flagged, and reported that the 2026 legislative season continued to degrade trans rights while federal policies drove nationwide trends.

Visa screening carries its own exposure. In February 2025 the State Department announced a ban on trans athletes entering the US to compete in women's sports, flagging visa applicants with an internal marking and treating applicants who list a gender other than their assigned sex as grounds for a permanent ban on grounds of fraud.

Federal custody presents documented harm. From 2026 the Federal Bureau of Prisons adopted Florida-based policies mandating conversion therapy for transgender inmates, including cutting hair short, withdrawing hormone medication, and substituting psychiatric therapy and drugs; imprisoned transgender people reported being denied care, and the Bureau stopped reporting the number of transgender prisoners held from 2025. In ICE custody, transgender men were reportedly subjected to forced-labour programmes, with refusals met by beatings, solitary confinement and reports of severe sexual abuse. In December 2025 the Attorney General instructed the FBI to offer cash bounties for information leading to the identification and arrest of transgender activists described as promoting "radical gender ideology" and characterised as "domestic terrorist groups"; a May 2026 White House counterterrorism strategy stated that activities would prioritise the identification and neutralisation of groups whose ideology is "anti-American, radically pro-transgender, and anarchist." Advocates have compared these actions to the early stages of genocide.

Care access is constrained for visitors needing it. Executive Order 14187 (January 2025) described gender-affirming care for minors as "chemical and surgical mutilation of children," leading some hospitals to pause care; in summer 2025 the Department of Justice subpoenaed over 20 hospitals for full records of patients under 19. In July 2025 the federal government shut down specialised LGBTQ youth services on the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline, and October 2025 proposed rules would bar Medicaid reimbursement for care to transgender patients under 18. Gender-affirming care for children is already banned in 27 states. Several of these federal measures have been blocked or enjoined in court.
tangentialFactors:
The District of Columbia's protective posture is contingent rather than self-executing. A July 2026 national legal risk assessment noted that DC may no longer be considered "most protective" because it can fall under attack from Congress and executive actions, while still listing DC among its Low-Risk jurisdictions alongside Arizona, Delaware, Maine, Michigan, Nevada, Pennsylvania, Virginia and Wisconsin.

Congress attached a bathroom ban to the District of Columbia, and on 5 December 2024 transgender-rights activists were arrested while protesting that measure at the Capitol, according to Axios. The District of Columbia has no state-level ban on trans use of facilities matching gender identity, placing it with 29 states and four territories in that category, but congressional and executive authority over DC means local protections can be overridden.
localsOnly:
Residents of the District of Columbia are not subject to the state-level bathroom bans and document restrictions affecting Kansas, Idaho and other states; DC has no ban on trans use of facilities matching gender identity. Local protections nonetheless sit beneath federal authority: Congress can attach riders to DC legislation, as it did with the bathroom ban protested in December 2024, and executive actions apply directly within the District.

DC residents holding passports, federal identity documents or visas face the same federal document and screening rules described for all US entry, including the X-marker processing halt and the visa-flagging of applicants who list a gender other than their assigned sex. Federal custody conditions reported for transgender prisoners and detained immigrants apply to people held in federal facilities regardless of DC residency.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the Supreme Court's November 2025 decision permitting the passport sex-marker restrictions will be revisited, and whether the ACLU suit on behalf of seven plaintiffs succeeds, remain unresolved in the sources.

The October 2025 proposed rules on Medicaid reimbursement for care to transgender patients under 18 are described as proposed; their final status is not sourced here. Several federal measures are noted as blocked or enjoined in court, but which specific orders remain in force as of the latest source date is not resolved.

The July 2026 assessment's characterisation of DC as no longer "most protective" rests on the general vulnerability of DC to congressional and executive action; no source in this inventory documents a specific post-2024 federal override of a DC trans-protection beyond the bathroom rider.
